displayQuote: Give me six lines written by the most honest of men, and I will find something in them to hang him

meta.title: Who really said "Give me six lines written by the most honest of men"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No 17th-century French source exists. The earliest located printing is 1782 — 140 years after Richelieu died — and it says ten lines and credits his interrogator Laubardemont. Richelieu's name is attached from 1790.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give me six lines written by the most honest of men'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Richelieu, on any evidence. Earliest printing: 1782, ten lines, credited to his agent Laubardemont. The line count wanders from one to ten — the signature of a saying with no original.

answer.label: Unknown — no 17th-century source exists
answer.authorDates: Earliest located printing 1782, in French · credited to Laubardemont, not Richelieu
answer.sourceLine: There is no 17th-century source of any kind — nothing survives from Richelieu’s own century that contains the line. The earliest located printing is from 1782, about 140 years after his death, and it does not say six lines and does not say Richelieu: it says ten lines and credits Jean Martin de Laubardemont, the magistrate Richelieu used for his most notorious prosecutions. Richelieu’s name is attached in 1790, during the Revolution, when a cardinal-minister was a convenient face for arbitrary justice.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Qu'on me donne dix lignes de l'écriture d'un homme, fût-ce à sa Maîtresse, & je suis sûr d'y trouver de quoi le faire pendre.
trail: The French sentence people quote today is ‘Qu’on me donne six lignes écrites de la main du plus honnête homme, j’y trouverai de quoi le faire pendre.’ It is real French and it circulates widely — but no 17th-century text contains it.

The earliest instance located in print is from 1782, in Lally-Tolendal’s introductory matter to a volume of correspondence, and it differs in both details that matter: ten lines, not six, and the speaker is Laubardemont, not Richelieu the French trail ↗.

In 1790 the remark is reassigned to Richelieu himself — now as a single line — in Dubois de Crancé’s Discours sur la force publique (1790, p. 3). Early 1800s criminal-trial records swing back to Laubardemont, but with six lines rather than ten.

The number will not stay still. Across the sources it is one, two, three, four, five, six and ten lines. A saying whose most memorable detail keeps changing is being retold from memory, not copied from a page.

Later scholarship keeps arriving at the same place. Édouard Fournier, in L’Esprit dans l’histoire (1867), judged that if anyone said it under Richelieu it was Laubardemont or Laffemas, his two prosecutors — Richelieu, he wrote, did not descend to the details of the executioner Fournier’s text ↗. David Hackett Fischer calls the modern form a paraphrase of Quintilian and finds nothing closer to Richelieu than the memoirs of Françoise Bertaut de Motteville — a memoirist Richelieu himself exiled from court, recalled only after his death in 1642, so no witness to his conversation the sourcing ↗.
source.excerptNote: The earliest located printing, from 1782, in the French of the period: ten lines rather than six, addressed to a mistress, and spoken by Laubardemont. Roughly: give me ten lines of any man's handwriting, even to his mistress, and I am sure to find enough in it to hang him. Note that the polished modern version is tighter and crueller — it has been improved in the retelling.
source.rightsNote: The 1782 and 1790 French printings are long out of copyright, as is Fournier’s 1867 discussion, so both the French text and the standard English rendering are free to reproduce. Modern translations published in the last few decades can carry a translator’s copyright of their own; the plain English version on this page is a common-form rendering with no single owner. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Cardinal Richelieu
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Richelieu
author.metaLine: 1585–1642 · Armand Jean du Plessis, chief minister to Louis XIII of France
author.bio: Cardinal Richelieu (1585–1642) ran France for Louis XIII for eighteen years, broke the political power of the Protestant towns and the great nobles, and founded the Académie française. He also built the machinery this saying describes — intercepted letters, special commissions, prosecutors like Laubardemont and Laffemas who could be relied on for a verdict. That is exactly why the line sticks to him: it is the right idea about his government attached to the wrong mouth. Dumas finished the job. The Richelieu most people picture is the villain of The Three Musketeers, and villains get the good lines.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabrication invented from nothing; it is an old French saying that drifted upward. It started attached to a prosecutor nobody remembers and ended attached to his famous employer.

items.why: Nothing in his memoirs, his political testament, his letters or any contemporary account of his conversation. The gap between his death in 1642 and the first printing in 1782 is about 140 years the French dossier ↗.

The magistrate Richelieu sent to try Urbain Grandier at Loudun — a man whose reputation for finding guilt was already proverbial. The earliest printing gives him the line, and says ten lines of a man’s handwriting, even to his mistress.

items.who: One, two, three, four, five, six, ten
items.why: Every version is confident and they disagree. That pattern is what oral transmission looks like: the shape of the idea survives, the specifics do not, and there is no manuscript to check any of them against.

Dumas dramatises the line as five lines in his 1842 novel Le Chevalier d’Harmental. Popular fiction like this is much of why the saying stuck to Richelieu the villain — and five is one more number the count never settles on the French dossier ↗.

The historian David Hackett Fischer reads the modern form as a paraphrase of the Roman rhetorician Quintilian on how any text can be turned against its writer. That is a lineage of thought, not a line of descent for the sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: An anonymous French saying with no 17th-century source. It first appears in print in 1782 — as ten lines, spoken by Laubardemont — and only becomes Richelieu’s in 1790 the French dossier ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It names a fear that has only got sharper: that the danger is not what you did but what you wrote, and that a sufficiently motivated reader can make any six lines mean something fatal. Everyone who has had an old email quoted back at them knows the feeling.

It also travels because it is a boast rather than a complaint. Put in the mouth of the man doing the hanging, it is far more chilling than any warning about arbitrary power written from outside — which is presumably why it climbed from an obscure magistrate to the most famous minister in French history.
detailsBody: 1642: Richelieu dies. Nothing resembling the saying appears in his own writings or in contemporary accounts of him.
1782: earliest located printing, in French, in Lally-Tolendal's introductory matter to a volume of correspondence — ten lines, spoken by Laubardemont.
1790: reassigned to Richelieu — now as a single line — in Dubois de Crancé's revolutionary Discours sur la force publique (p. 3).
Early 1800s: criminal-trial records credit Laubardemont again, now with six lines.
1867: Édouard Fournier concludes that if anyone said it, it was Laubardemont or Laffemas — not Richelieu.
1896: the English form is carried into Hoyt's Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations, which is how most English speakers meet it.
context.pull: Ten lines in 1782, six by 1800. The number moves — which is how you know nobody was reading it off a page.
